why_how.text: Right-of-way rules exist so drivers and pedestrians know who goes first where no sign or signal decides.
The law only says who must yield, so even a driver with a green light must let others already in the intersection finish.

scenario.text: Pia's light turns green just as a pedestrian is finishing a slow crossing in front of her car.

reasoning.text: A green light lets you go but does not give you the right of way; anyone already in the intersection still goes first.

result.text: Pia waits for the pedestrian to reach the curb, then drives on.

claim.text: Many people think a green light gives them the right of way over everyone.

correction.text: The law never grants anyone the right of way, not even on a green light; it only says who must yield.

memory_support.text: Law says who yields, never who owns.

prompt.text: Your light turns green while a bicyclist is still crossing in front of you. Who goes first?

rationale.text: You must yield to anyone already inside the intersection, and a green light does not change that.

narration.text: This chapter is about right of way: who goes first and who waits. Many crashes happen not because someone broke a speed limit, but because two people each believed the other would wait. This first lesson lays the foundation. You will learn what right-of-way rules decide, why the law only says who must yield rather than who owns the road, the duty to yield to anyone already in an intersection, and the rule that sits above all the others: every driver must try to avoid a crash, whoever was supposed to go first. Keep that last rule in mind through every scenario in this chapter.

lines.text: Who goes first and who waits.
Where no sign or signal controls traffic.

narration.text: Right-of-way rules decide who goes first and who waits when drivers or pedestrians meet where no sign or signal controls traffic. At a busy signal, the lights do most of the work. But many meetings happen where nothing controls traffic: an uncontrolled intersection, a parking lot exit, a narrow road, a merge. In those places, right-of-way rules are what keep traffic orderly. They work only when everyone knows and follows them. That is why the knowledge test includes so many right-of-way questions, and why each one usually describes a specific meeting point and asks who should wait for whom.

lines.text: The law says who must yield.
It never grants the right of way.
Not even on a green light.

narration.text: The law only says who must yield. It never grants anyone the right of way, not even a driver facing a green light. That wording matters. It means you can never insist on going first. The rules tell you when you must wait, and when the other person is expected to wait, but they never promise that the other person will. You must also yield to pedestrians, bicyclists and drivers who are already inside an intersection you are approaching. Arriving at an intersection does not give you a claim over people who are already using it.

title.text: Green is not right of way

lines.text: It does not make you first.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A green light lets you go, but it does not give you the right of way. Anyone already in the intersection still goes first. Picture a driver finishing a left turn as your light changes, or a pedestrian walking slowly who has not yet reached the curb. You must let them clear before you move. Practice questions often describe a driver who pulls forward on green and strikes someone still in the intersection, then ask who should have yielded. The answer is the driver with the green light, because a green light is permission to proceed, not ownership of the space.

lines.text: No matter who has the right of way.
Every driver must avoid a crash.

narration.text: No matter who has the right of way, every driver is still responsible for avoiding a crash. If another driver fails to yield to you, you must still brake, steer or do whatever you safely can to prevent a collision. Being technically right does not undo an injury. This rule ties all the others together. The yielding rules tell you what to expect from others, but you should always be ready for someone to get it wrong, especially at intersections, merges and crosswalks. Defensive drivers look for mistakes and leave themselves room to react when someone else does not wait.

Here is a quick check: you are first in line at a red light. It turns green, but a bicyclist who entered on the last yellow is still crossing in front of you. Who goes first? Decide before reading on. The bicyclist goes first. You must yield to pedestrians, bicyclists and drivers who are already inside an intersection you are approaching, and a green light lets you go but never gives you the right of way. Even if the bicyclist had made a mistake, you would still be responsible for doing what you can to avoid a crash.

Let us review. Right-of-way rules decide who goes first and who waits where no sign or signal controls traffic. The law only says who must yield; it never grants anyone the right of way, not even a driver facing a green light. You must yield to pedestrians, bicyclists and drivers already inside an intersection you are approaching. And no matter who has the right of way, every driver is still responsible for avoiding a crash. With these basics in place, the next lesson turns to the most vulnerable road users: pedestrians and bicyclists.

why_how.text: Pedestrians and bicyclists have little protection, so drivers carry the duty to yield and take extra care.
Whether a bicyclist is treated as a vehicle or a pedestrian depends on where they are riding.

scenario.text: Noah is about to turn right across a bike lane when a bicyclist approaches in that lane from behind.

reasoning.text: When you merge with or cross a designated bike lane to turn, you must yield to bicyclists in it.

result.text: Noah lets the bicyclist pass, checks again, then crosses the bike lane and turns.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a bicyclist in a crosswalk must be treated like a car.

correction.text: A bicyclist on the roadway is treated as a vehicle, but the same rider in a crosswalk or on a sidewalk is treated as a pedestrian.

memory_support.text: Road rider vehicle, crosswalk rider pedestrian.

prompt.text: A bicyclist rides slowly across a crosswalk in front of you. How should you treat the rider?

answer.text: As a pedestrian, with the rights and duties of a pedestrian.

rationale.text: On the road a bicycle is a vehicle, but in a crosswalk or on a sidewalk the rider is treated as a pedestrian.

narration.text: This lesson focuses on the road users most likely to be hurt in a collision: pedestrians and bicyclists. You will learn the rule that drivers always yield to pedestrians at intersections and crosswalks, which pedestrians need extra care, how to recognize a pedestrian who is blind or deaf-blind, how the law treats a bicycle on the road compared with a bicyclist on a sidewalk, and what to do when your turn crosses a bike lane. In every case, the driver of the car is the one with the most protection, and therefore the one expected to take the most care.

lines.text: Pedestrians have the right of way.
Stop fully and let them pass.

narration.text: Drivers must always yield to pedestrians, who have the right of way at every intersection and crosswalk. Come to a full stop and let them pass safely. Do not creep forward or try to steer around someone who is crossing. Take extra care around children, seniors and people with disabilities, who may move unpredictably or more slowly. And never assume a pedestrian can see or hear your vehicle or a crossing signal. Someone looking at a phone, wearing headphones or with limited vision may step into the road without noticing you, so your attention has to make up for theirs.

lines.text: Usual sign of a blind or deaf-blind walker.

narration.text: A white cane or a guide dog is the usual sign that a pedestrian is blind or deaf-blind. When you see one, stop and give the person plenty of time and space to cross. Do not honk, rev your engine or wave, because they may not see or hear it, and sudden noises can be confusing or alarming. Remember the broader rule from the last slide: never assume a pedestrian can see or hear your vehicle. With a white cane or guide dog, you can be fairly sure they cannot see you, so it is entirely up to you to stop and wait until they have finished crossing.

lines.text: A bicycle on the road is a vehicle.
Many rights and duties of a motor vehicle.
Yield to riders in bike lanes when turning.

narration.text: On the road a bicycle counts as a vehicle, with many of the rights and duties of a motor vehicle. Bicyclists must follow traffic rules, and drivers must share the road with them. When you merge with or cross a designated bike lane to make a turn, you must yield to bicyclists in that lane. This is especially important for right turns, where a bicyclist may be coming up on your right in the bike lane. Check your mirror and look over your shoulder before you move into or across the bike lane, and let any bicyclist pass before you turn.

lines.text: In a crosswalk or on a sidewalk: a pedestrian.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A bicyclist on the roadway is treated as a vehicle, but the same rider in a crosswalk or on a sidewalk is treated as a pedestrian. So the rules you apply depend on where the bicyclist is at that moment. A bicyclist riding in the travel lane follows vehicle rules, and you treat them like another slow vehicle. A bicyclist crossing in a crosswalk has the rights and duties of a pedestrian, so you yield as you would to someone walking. Questions test this by placing the rider in a crosswalk and asking whether vehicle or pedestrian rules apply.

lines.text: A bicyclist crossing in a crosswalk.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are stopped at an intersection, ready to turn right, when a bicyclist rides slowly across the crosswalk in front of you. Should you treat the rider as a vehicle or as a pedestrian? Think it through before reading on. As a pedestrian. A bicyclist on a sidewalk or in a crosswalk has the rights and duties of a pedestrian, so you yield and let them cross. If the same bicyclist were riding in the travel lane, they would be treated as a vehicle. And if your turn crossed a bike lane, you would yield to riders in that lane too.

lines.text: Bicycle: vehicle on road, pedestrian in crosswalk.

narration.text: Let us review. Drivers must always yield to pedestrians, who have the right of way at every intersection and crosswalk; come to a full stop and let them pass safely. Take extra care around children, seniors and people with disabilities, and never assume a pedestrian can see or hear you. A white cane or guide dog usually means a pedestrian is blind or deaf-blind. On the road a bicycle is a vehicle, but a bicyclist on a sidewalk or in a crosswalk is treated as a pedestrian. When merging with or crossing a bike lane to turn, yield to bicyclists in it. Next, intersections and left turns.

why_how.text: Simple tie-break rules prevent standoffs and collisions when drivers arrive at the same time.
Left turns cross oncoming traffic, which is why the turning driver usually yields.

scenario.text: Eli and another driver reach a four-way stop at the same moment; the other driver is on Eli's right.

reasoning.text: When vehicles arrive together at a four-way stop, the one on the left yields to the one on the right.

result.text: Eli lets the driver on his right go first, then proceeds.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the tie-break at an uncontrolled intersection differs from the one at a four-way stop.

correction.text: Both share the same tie-break: when two arrive together, the driver on the left waits for the driver on the right.

prompt.text: At an intersection with no signs or signals, you and another car arrive at once, and the other car is on your left. Who goes first?

answer.text: You do, because you are on the right.

rationale.text: The vehicle on the left lets the vehicle on the right go first, the same tie-break as at a four-way stop.

narration.text: Intersections are where most right-of-way decisions happen. This lesson covers the four-way stop, the uncontrolled intersection with no signs or lights at all, and the rules for turning left, which is one of the riskiest moves at any intersection. You will see that four-way stops and uncontrolled intersections share the same tie-break rule, which makes them easier to remember. We will also connect left turns to the diverging diamond interchange from the last chapter, because that design exists to remove the most troublesome left-turn conflicts at freeway interchanges.

lines.text: Arrive together: left yields to right.

narration.text: At a four-way stop, the first vehicle to arrive goes first. Every driver comes to a full stop, then the drivers proceed in the order they arrived. If vehicles arrive together, the one on the left yields to the one on the right. So when you and another driver stop at the same moment and the other car is on your right, you let them go first. If the other car is on your left, you go first. Making eye contact and moving predictably helps, but the rule is what settles a tie. A dark or broken signal, as you learned, is also handled as a four-way stop.

lines.text: Arrive together: left yields to right.

narration.text: An uncontrolled intersection has no stop signs or lights. These are common in older neighborhoods and rural areas. When vehicles reach it at the same moment, the vehicle on the left lets the vehicle on the right go first. Because there is no sign telling you to stop, approach these intersections at a speed that lets you stop if needed, and look both ways early. If another vehicle is clearly already in the intersection, yield to it, just as you would anywhere else. The tie-break only settles cases where both vehicles arrive at the same time.

lines.text: Four-way stop tie: left yields to right.
Uncontrolled tie: left yields to right.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Learners sometimes memorize two different rules for four-way stops and uncontrolled intersections, then mix them up. In fact they share the same tie-break: when two arrive together, the driver on the left waits for the driver on the right. Questions may describe one kind of intersection and offer the opposite tie-break as a tempting answer, such as letting the driver on the left go first. Remember one rule for both: a tie goes to the right. What differs is only that a four-way stop requires everyone to stop first, while an uncontrolled intersection has no stop signs.

lines.text: Yield to all oncoming traffic unless arrow or first.

narration.text: Before turning left, yield to pedestrians in the crosswalk and to smaller oncoming road users like bicyclists and motorcyclists, judging their speed and distance carefully. Smaller vehicles are harder to see and their speed is harder to judge, so take an extra look. A left-turning driver yields to all oncoming traffic unless holding a green arrow or having arrived first at a four-way stop. A diverging diamond interchange removes the troublesome left-turn movements of a standard interchange, which leaves fewer conflict points with other vehicles. That design shows how risky ordinary left turns are.

lines.text: The other car is on your left.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you reach a neighborhood intersection with no signs or signals at the same moment as another car. The other car is on your left. Who goes first? Decide before reading on. You do. At an uncontrolled intersection, when vehicles arrive together, the vehicle on the left lets the vehicle on the right go first, and you are on the right. A four-way stop uses the same tie-break. If you were turning left, though, you would still need to yield to oncoming traffic unless you held a green arrow or had arrived first at a four-way stop.

Let us review. At a four-way stop the first vehicle to arrive goes first, and if vehicles arrive together the one on the left yields to the one on the right. An uncontrolled intersection has no stop signs or lights and uses the same tie-break. Before turning left, yield to pedestrians in the crosswalk and smaller oncoming users like bicyclists and motorcyclists, and yield to all oncoming traffic unless you hold a green arrow or arrived first at a four-way stop. A diverging diamond interchange removes troublesome left-turn movements, leaving fewer conflict points. Next, lane changes and merging.

why_how.text: Yielding when you change lanes, merge or back up keeps you from forcing others to brake suddenly.
On a narrow steep road, the downhill driver usually has better control to back up or wait.

scenario.text: On a narrow mountain road, Rae is driving downhill when an uphill car appears with no room to pass.

reasoning.text: The downhill driver yields by backing to a wider spot or stopping to leave room, unless the uphill driver can more practically reach a turnout.

result.text: Rae backs to a wider spot so the uphill car can pass.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the uphill vehicle always yields on a narrow mountain road.

correction.text: The downhill vehicle normally yields, unless the uphill vehicle can more practically reach a turnout.

prompt.text: You are driving downhill on a road too narrow for two vehicles, and a car is coming uphill. Who normally yields?

answer.text: You do, as the downhill driver.

rationale.text: The downhill driver normally yields, unless the uphill driver can more practically reach a turnout.

narration.text: Whenever you move into a space someone else is using or about to use, you take on a duty to yield. This lesson covers changing lanes and passing, merging onto a road, backing up, and a special Colorado situation: meeting another vehicle on a steep road too narrow for two. The common thread is that the driver making the move is usually the one who waits. That keeps traffic predictable, because drivers already in a lane can trust that others will not cut them off. Mountain roads add a twist that is easy to get backward, so we will look at it closely.

lines.text: Yield to vehicles already in the lane.
Do not move over if someone must slow.

narration.text: When changing lanes or passing, yield to vehicles already in the lane you want. Do not move over if another driver would have to slow for you. A signal tells others what you intend, but it does not give you the space. Before moving, check your mirrors and look over your shoulder into your blind spot, then move only when there is a gap large enough that no one has to brake. Cutting in close in front of another vehicle is a common cause of rear-end crashes, especially at highway speeds, where the driver behind may have very little time to react.

lines.text: Merging: yield to every vehicle on the road.
Do not force anyone to slow.

narration.text: When merging, yield to every vehicle on the road you are joining, and do not merge if it would force someone to slow down. Use the on-ramp or acceleration lane to match the speed of traffic and find a gap. When backing up, yield to all vehicles near enough to be a hazard. Backing is slow and your view is limited, so other drivers may not expect you to move. Whether you are merging or backing, the driver entering the flow of traffic is the one who waits. Only move when you are sure you will not force anyone to brake or swerve.

lines.text: Downhill yields: back up or stop.
Unless uphill can reach a turnout.

narration.text: On a steep road too narrow for two vehicles, the downhill driver yields by backing to a wider spot or stopping to leave room. The exception is when it is more practical for the uphill driver to return to a turnout. The reasoning is about control. A vehicle going uphill may struggle to restart on a steep grade, and backing downhill is often harder and more dangerous than backing uphill. These roads are common in Colorado's mountains, so it is worth knowing the rule before you meet another car around a blind curve with no room to pass.

lines.text: Uphill only if a turnout is closer.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers guess that the uphill vehicle should yield, perhaps because it is moving more slowly. The handbook says the opposite. On a narrow mountain road the downhill vehicle is the one that normally yields, not the uphill one. The only exception is when the uphill vehicle can more practically reach a turnout. Questions may describe two cars meeting on a narrow grade and offer the uphill driver as the one who must back up. Unless the scenario mentions a nearby turnout behind the uphill car, the downhill driver is the one who gives way.

Here is a quick check: you are driving downhill on a steep mountain road too narrow for two vehicles, and a car appears coming uphill. There is no turnout behind the other car. Who normally yields, and how? Decide before reading on. You do. The downhill driver yields by backing to a wider spot or stopping to leave room. The uphill driver would yield only if it were more practical for them to return to a turnout. The same idea of yielding applies elsewhere too: when changing lanes, merging or backing, the driver moving into others' space waits.

lines.text: Yield to the lane you want.
Merge and back without forcing slowdowns.

narration.text: Let us review. When changing lanes or passing, yield to vehicles already in the lane you want, and do not move over if another driver would have to slow. When merging, yield to every vehicle on the road you are joining. When backing up, yield to all vehicles near enough to be a hazard. On a steep road too narrow for two vehicles, the downhill driver yields by backing to a wider spot or stopping, unless the uphill driver can more practically reach a turnout. Next, we look at emergency vehicles and how to move over for them.

why_how.text: Pulling over for emergency vehicles clears a path for people racing to save lives.
Moving over for stopped emergency vehicles protects responders working beside fast traffic.

scenario.text: On a highway posted at sixty-five, Ivy approaches a police car stopped on the shoulder, and heavy traffic blocks her from changing lanes.

reasoning.text: If you cannot leave an empty lane, slow down; above forty-five, the speed is twenty under the limit.

result.text: Ivy slows to forty-five as she passes the police car, then resumes speed.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you must pull over and stop for an emergency vehicle that is already stopped on the shoulder.

correction.text: You pull right and stop for an approaching emergency vehicle, but for one already stopped you leave a lane open or slow as you pass.

memory_support.text: Coming: pull over. Stopped: move over.

prompt.text: A fire truck with its siren on comes up behind you while you are halfway through an intersection. What should you do?

answer.text: Continue through the intersection first, then pull over.

rationale.text: Stopping inside the intersection would block the fire truck; clear it, then pull to the right edge and stop.

narration.text: Emergency vehicles need a clear path, and the people working beside them on the road need space and slower traffic to stay safe. This lesson covers both situations. First, what to do when an emergency vehicle approaches with a siren, air horn or flashing lights, including the special case when you are already inside an intersection. Second, what to do when you pass an emergency vehicle stopped beside the road, including the speed rule when you cannot change lanes. The two responses are different, and practice questions often test whether you can tell them apart.

lines.text: Siren, air horn or flashing lights.
Red, blue, white or yellow lights.
Pull right and stop where possible.

narration.text: Yield to any emergency vehicle using a siren, an air horn, or flashing red, blue, white or yellow lights. Pull to the right edge of the road and stop where possible. Stay stopped until the emergency vehicle has passed, and watch for others that may be following it. Do not slam on your brakes in your lane or swerve suddenly; signal and move right smoothly. On a multi-lane road, every lane of traffic moves right. If you cannot pull fully to the edge because of parked cars or a curb, move as far right as you safely can and stop so the emergency vehicle can get by.

If an emergency vehicle approaches while you are inside an intersection, continue through the intersection first and then pull over. Stopping in the middle of an intersection would block the emergency vehicle's path and could trap it, and it can also confuse cross traffic. So finish crossing, then pull to the right edge and stop as soon as you safely can. This is one of the few times the handbook tells you to keep moving when an emergency vehicle appears, and it is easy to get wrong under pressure. Clear the intersection, then make way.

lines.text: Leave at least one empty lane.
Or slow to a safe speed.

narration.text: When passing an emergency vehicle stopped beside the road, try to leave at least one empty lane between you and it. If you cannot change lanes, slow to a safe speed and use care as you pass. Unless emergency personnel direct otherwise or conditions prevent a lane change, slow to twenty-five miles per hour when the posted limit is forty-five or less, or to twenty miles per hour below the limit when it is above forty-five. Responders at the roadside are often focused on a crash or a stopped driver, and a passing car only a few feet away can be deadly.

lines.text: Stopped at the roadside: move over or slow.

narration.text: Here is the first trap. The response to an emergency vehicle depends on whether it is moving toward you or already stopped. For an approaching emergency vehicle, you pull right and stop. For one already stopped at the roadside, you leave a lane open or slow down as you pass. Mixing them up is dangerous. Stopping on a highway next to a stopped police car creates a new hazard, while merely moving over for an ambulance racing up behind you leaves it stuck. Questions describe one situation and offer the other response, so check whether the vehicle is coming or stopped.

lines.text: Limit forty-five or less: slow to twenty-five.

narration.text: Here is the second trap. The move-over speed depends on the posted limit. At forty-five miles per hour or below, slow to twenty-five. Above forty-five, slow to twenty miles per hour under the limit. So on a road posted at forty, slow to twenty-five, and on a highway posted at sixty-five, slow to forty-five. Questions often swap the two rules, offering twenty under the limit on a slow road or twenty-five on a fast highway. Check the posted limit first, then apply the matching rule. Remember too that this speed applies when you cannot leave an empty lane.

Here is a quick check: you are halfway through an intersection on a green light when a fire truck with its siren on comes up behind you. What should you do? Decide before reading on. Continue through the intersection first, then pull to the right edge and stop where possible. Stopping in the intersection would block the fire truck. Later, if you pass that same fire truck stopped beside the road, try to leave an empty lane, or slow down: to twenty-five at limits of forty-five or less, or to twenty under faster limits.

lines.text: In an intersection: clear it first.
Stopped: empty lane or slow down.

narration.text: Let us review. Yield to any emergency vehicle using a siren, air horn or flashing red, blue, white or yellow lights by pulling to the right edge and stopping where possible. If you are inside an intersection, continue through first, then pull over. When passing an emergency vehicle stopped beside the road, try to leave at least one empty lane, or slow to a safe speed. Unless directed otherwise, slow to twenty-five when the limit is forty-five or less, or to twenty below the limit above forty-five. Next, service vehicles, snow plows and work zones.

why_how.text: Service crews work close to moving traffic, so drivers must yield and pass with extra care.
Snow plows create their own visibility problems, which is why passing staggered plows is illegal.

scenario.text: During a snowstorm, Ben comes up behind three snow plows staggered diagonally across the highway.

reasoning.text: Snow plows can be hidden by blowing snow, and passing working plows staggered in formation is illegal.

result.text: Ben stays well back behind the plows and follows them on the cleared road.

claim.text: Common mistake: assuming any vehicle with flashing yellow and blue lights is an emergency vehicle.

correction.text: Maintenance vehicles use flashing yellow and blue lights, while emergency vehicles may use red, blue, white or yellow lights with a siren or air horn.

memory_support.text: Yellow and blue means a working crew.

prompt.text: You see a truck working on the shoulder with flashing yellow and blue lights. What kind of vehicle is it, and what do you do?

answer.text: A service or maintenance vehicle; yield and take extra care passing it.

rationale.text: Yellow and blue flashing lights mark maintenance vehicles, while emergency vehicles may use red, blue, white or yellow lights with a siren.

narration.text: Not every vehicle with flashing lights is an ambulance or police car. Road crews, tow operators and maintenance trucks also work beside and in traffic, and they need drivers to slow down and give them room. This lesson covers how to treat working service vehicles, how to tell their lights from emergency lights, why snow plows are so dangerous to pass, and how to drive through a work zone. In each case, the people on foot near the road are exposed, and your speed and lane position are what keep them safe while they do their jobs.

Yield to service and maintenance vehicles that are working and showing flashing yellow and blue lights, and take extra care when approaching or passing them. These vehicles may be stopped, moving slowly, or pulling in and out of traffic. Workers may step out unexpectedly to place cones or check equipment. Slow down early, watch for people near the vehicle, and leave extra space as you pass. If you can move over a lane safely, do so. The flashing lights are a signal that people are working nearby, not just a vehicle parked on the shoulder.

lines.text: Emergency: red, blue, white or yellow with siren or air horn.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Maintenance vehicles use flashing yellow and blue lights, while emergency vehicles may use red, blue, white or yellow lights with a siren or air horn. Because yellow and blue appear in both lists, learners sometimes treat every flashing vehicle the same way. The difference matters: for an approaching emergency vehicle you pull right and stop, while for a working maintenance vehicle you yield and pass with extra care. Look for the combination of yellow and blue lights on a work truck, and listen for a siren or air horn, which signals an emergency vehicle.

lines.text: Hidden by their own blowing snow.
Never pass plows staggered in formation.

narration.text: Snow plows can be hidden by the blowing snow they throw up, so you may come upon one suddenly in a storm. Slow down whenever visibility drops and you see flashing lights ahead. Passing working plows that are staggered diagonally in formation is illegal. Plows often work in a diagonal line across several lanes to clear a whole highway at once, and a car trying to slip between them can be struck or buried in snow. Stay well back. The road behind the plows is usually the safest road available in a storm, so following them is often the smartest choice.

lines.text: Shift your lane position away from workers.

narration.text: In a work or construction zone, protect crews and other road users by shifting your lane position away from workers and slowing down for obstacles. Lanes may be narrow, shifted or closed, and the pavement may be uneven. Workers may be just a few feet from traffic. Moving to the side of your lane away from the crew gives them a little more space, and a slower speed gives you time to react to equipment, debris or sudden lane changes. Remember the orange work zone signs from earlier: they warn you to expect these conditions well before you reach the workers.

Here is a quick check: on a highway, you see a truck working on the shoulder with flashing yellow and blue lights and no siren. What kind of vehicle is it, and how should you respond? Think it through before reading on. It is a service or maintenance vehicle. Yield to it and take extra care as you approach and pass, moving over if you can. Emergency vehicles may use red, blue, white or yellow lights with a siren or air horn. And if the vehicles ahead were snow plows staggered across the lanes, passing them would be illegal.

lines.text: Shift away and slow in work zones.

narration.text: Let us review. Yield to service and maintenance vehicles that are working and showing flashing yellow and blue lights, and take extra care when approaching or passing them. Emergency vehicles may use red, blue, white or yellow lights with a siren or air horn. Snow plows can be hidden by the snow they throw up, and passing working plows staggered diagonally in formation is illegal. In work or construction zones, shift your lane position away from workers and slow down for obstacles. Next, we finish the chapter with school buses and transit buses.

why_how.text: Children getting on and off school buses are hard to see and may cross unexpectedly, so traffic in both directions stops.
Yielding to transit buses helps them pull back into traffic safely and keeps service on schedule.

scenario.text: On an undivided two-lane road, Sam is driving toward a school bus that stops on the opposite side with red lights flashing.

reasoning.text: The stop rule applies on the opposite side too, unless a median or other physical barrier separates you from the bus.

result.text: Sam stops at least twenty feet from the bus, waits until the lights stop flashing, then looks for children before moving.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking drivers on the other side of the road never have to stop for a school bus.

correction.text: The school bus stop applies in both directions; only a median or other physical barrier between you and the bus excuses you.

memory_support.text: Both ways stop, unless a barrier.

prompt.text: A school bus stops with red lights flashing on the other side of an undivided road. Must you stop?

answer.text: Yes, at least twenty feet away, until the lights stop flashing.

rationale.text: Only a median or other physical barrier between you and the bus would excuse you from stopping.

narration.text: This final lesson of the chapter covers buses. School buses get special treatment because children getting on and off are small, hard to see and may dart across the road without looking. You will learn how far back to stop, how long to stay stopped, which drivers must stop, the one situation that excuses you, and what to do when the lights turn off. Then we look at transit buses, which have their own yield rule when they pull back into traffic. School bus rules are among the most important on the test, and among the most serious to break in real life.

lines.text: Stay stopped until they stop flashing.

narration.text: Stop at least twenty feet away from a school bus that has stopped with red lights flashing, and stay stopped until the lights stop flashing. The twenty-foot gap gives children room to cross in front of or beside the bus, and gives you a clear view of them. Do not inch forward while you wait. The flashing red lights mean children are getting on or off, or crossing. When the bus driver turns off the red lights, that is the signal that the stop is over, but as you will see, it is not yet a signal to drive off without looking.

The school bus stop rule applies on your side of the road, on the opposite side, or at an intersection ahead. In other words, traffic in both directions stops, along with traffic approaching from cross streets at an intersection where the bus has stopped. The exception is when a median or other physical barrier separates you from the bus. A painted center line or a center turn lane is not a physical barrier. The point of the rule is that children may cross to either side of the road, so any driver who could reach them must stop.

lines.text: A median or physical barrier is the only exception.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers think only traffic behind a school bus must stop. The school bus stop applies in both directions, and only a median or other physical barrier between you and the bus excuses you from stopping. Questions might describe a four-lane road with no barrier and ask whether oncoming drivers must stop. They must. Other questions describe a divided highway with a raised median, where oncoming drivers may continue. The deciding question is simple: is there a physical barrier between you and the bus? If not, you stop.

lines.text: Look for children near the bus.

narration.text: After a school bus turns off its lights, look carefully for children near the bus and crossing the road before you move. A child who dropped something, or who is late, may still be in the road even after the lights stop. Children can also be hidden by the bus itself, especially on the far side. So when the lights go off, check all around before you start, and move slowly at first. This step completes the school bus routine: stop at least twenty feet back while lights flash, stay stopped until they stop, and then look for children before moving.

lines.text: Bus signaling to pull into traffic.
Yield sign on its rear is lit.

narration.text: Yield to a transit bus that is signaling to pull into a traffic lane when the yield sign on its rear is lit. This is a reversal of the usual merging rule, where the driver entering traffic yields. For transit buses, drivers already in the lane let the bus back in. The lit yield sign tells you the bus is ready to move. Slow down and leave a gap so the bus can pull out safely. Doing so helps keep buses on schedule and prevents crashes, since a bus pulling out has limited acceleration and a large blind area beside it.

Here is a quick check: you are driving on an undivided two-lane road when a school bus coming toward you stops on the opposite side with its red lights flashing. Must you stop, and if so, where and for how long? Decide before reading on. Yes, you must stop, at least twenty feet from the bus, and stay stopped until the lights stop flashing. The rule applies on the opposite side of the road too; only a median or other physical barrier between you and the bus would excuse you. After the lights go off, look carefully for children before you move.

lines.text: Twenty feet; wait for lights off.
Yield to transit buses pulling in.

narration.text: Let us close the chapter. Stop at least twenty feet from a school bus stopped with red lights flashing, and stay stopped until the lights stop. The rule applies on your side, the opposite side or at an intersection ahead, unless a median or other physical barrier separates you from the bus. After the lights go off, look carefully for children near the bus and crossing before you move. Yield to a transit bus signaling to pull into traffic when the yield sign on its rear is lit. With right of way covered, you are ready for speed, turning and parking.
